title: Heat and cold
hookLine: Krishna: pleasure and pain come and go like heat and cold; bear them

lines: THE COLD HITS LIKE A SLAP.
BY EVENING, THE HEAT IS GONE.
cards: Step out of a warm house into a winter morning and the cold hits like a slap. A little way into the walk, you've half forgotten it. A summer afternoon's heat presses down; by evening a breeze comes and it's gone.
Nobody takes the weather personally for long. It arrives, it stays a while, it leaves. In the Gita, Arjuna has just said I will not fight and fallen silent.
The text says Krishna answers him, as if smiling. And early in that answer, he reaches for the weather.

teach.h: PLEASURE AND PAIN COME AND GO.
teach.b: In the second chapter of the Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that the touch of the senses on the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. The Sanskrit calls these matra-sparsha, the contacts of the senses.
Second, what they do. They come and go, Krishna says. They don't last.
The verse takes things we'd usually sort into good and bad, pleasure and pain, and gives them the same nature: arriving, and leaving. Third, the instruction.
Bear them, Arjuna. The Sanskrit word is titikshasva: bear it, put up with it. Not enjoy it, not deny it.

Stay standing while it passes through. The next verse names the reward: the steady person whom these don't throw off balance, the same in pain and pleasure, is fit, Krishna says, for what doesn't die.
Fourth, what it isn't. This isn't a teaching that pain is unreal, or that Arjuna's grief is foolish.
Krishna is speaking to a man slumped on a chariot seat, and he starts small, with a picture: feelings, even huge ones, are like weather.
Hindu teachers read this verse in different ways, some as a first step toward knowing the self, some as training for steady action. Each reading starts from the same line.
What arrives can be borne, partly because it will also leave.

how: Some Hindu teachers point to Gita 2.14 when teaching steadiness in pleasure and pain, and some practices of fasting, austerity and meditation are understood as training in this endurance, titiksha.

o: Krishna's word: bear it, stay steady while it passes
Krishna's word: pretend the pain isn't really there
Krishna's word: fight back until the pain is gone

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: Krishna's picture for pleasure and pain
the same in pain and pleasure

s: in this verse, Krishna says pain is unreal
he says pleasure and pain come and go, and asks Arjuna to bear them.
the verse gives pleasure and pain the same nature
both arrive and leave, like heat and cold.
Krishna answers Arjuna's despair with anger
the text says he speaks as if smiling.

games.q: you're Krishna. your friend has sunk down on the chariot seat, refusing to fight. what's the first picture you give him?
o: a story of a great victory.
the weather: heat and cold that come and go.
games.why: Krishna says the contacts of the senses bring cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they come and go. bear them.

practice: Notice one small discomfort already present, an itch, a stiff shoulder, cool air on your hands, and don't fix it; bear it, the way Krishna asks. Watch it closely: does it stay exactly the same, or shift, rise, fade, come back?
You're not fighting it and not giving in to it, just staying standing while it passes through.

wordCard.voice: Titikshasva, Krishna's Sanskrit word in the Gita for bearing heat and cold, pleasure and pain, without being thrown off balance. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Gita 2.14: bear them, endure them; the noun is titikṣā, endurance.

carryVoice: Your line: they come and go. Heat and cold, pleasure and pain, like weather. Day seven hundred twenty-five, done.
